i
CAPITAL CASE
QUESTION PRESENTED
In lieu of Petitioner’s question presented, Respondent suggests:
Whether a claim is “previously unavailable” for the purpose of authorizing a
successive federal habeas petition when the claim had no possibility of merit while
the first habeas petition was pending.

ii
PARTIES TO THE P ROCEEDING AND
RULE 29.6 S TATEMENT
Petitioner is Eric Guerrero, Director of the Texas Department of Criminal
Justice, Correctional Institutions Division.
Respondent is Dexter Johnson.
There are no corporate parties involved in this case.

iii
RULE 14.1(b )(iii) STATEMENT
This case arises from the following proceedings in the Texas Court of Criminal
Appeals, the United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas,  the
United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit , and the Supreme Court of the
United States:
Johnson v. State, No. AP-75,749, Texas Court of Criminal Appeals. Judgment
affirming conviction and death sentence entered January 27, 2010.
Johnson v. Texas , No. 09 -10475, Supreme Court of the United States. Order
denying petition for writ of certiorari entered June 28, 2010.
Ex parte Johnson, No. WR-73,600-01, Texas Court of Criminal Appeals. Order
denying initial state habeas application entered June 30, 2010.
Johnson v. Stephens , No. H -11-2466, United States District Court for the
Southern District of Texas. Order denying habeas relief entered August 19, 2013.
Johnson v. Stephens , No. H -11-2466, United States District Court for the
Southern District of Texas. Order denying motion for reconsideration entered October
10, 2013.
Johnson v. Stephens , No. H -11-2466, United States District Court for the
Southern District of Texas. Order denying habeas relief entered June 25, 2014.
Johnson v. Stephens , No. 14 -70024, United States Court of Appeals for the
Fifth Circuit. Judgment affirming denial of habeas relief entered July 2, 2015.
Johnson v. Stephens, No. 15-6401, Supreme Court of the United States. Order
denying petition for writ of certiorari entered January 25, 2016.
Johnson v. Davis , No. H -11-2466, United States District Court for the
Southern District of Texas. Order denying motion for reconsideration entered
November 6, 2017.
Johnson v. Davis, No. 17-70032, United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth
Circuit. Order denying certificate of appealability entered August 24, 2018.
Johnson v. Stephens, No. 18–6834, Supreme Court of the United States. Order
denying petition for writ of certiorari entered March 25, 2019.
Ex parte Johnson, No. WR-75,478-02, Texas Court of Criminal Appeals. Order
dismissing successive state habeas application entered April 29, 2019.

iv
Ex parte Johnson, No. WR-73,600-03, Texas Court of Criminal Appeals. Order
dismissing successive state habeas application entered August 13, 2019.
In re Johnson, No. 19 -20552, United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth
Circuit. Order authorizing second or successive habeas application entered August
14, 2019.
Johnson v. Stephens, No. 19-6934, Supreme Court of the United States. Order
denying petition for writ of certiorari entered March 23, 2020.
Johnson v. Lumpkin, No. 4:19 -cv-3047, United States District Court for the
Southern District of Texas. Memorandum and order on successiveness and denying
Director’s motion to dismiss entered October 28, 2022.
Johnson v. Lumpkin, No. 4:19 -cv-3047, United States District Court for the
Southern District of Texas. Order certifying interlocutory appeal entered January 12,
2023.
Lumpkin v. Johnson , No. 23 -90003, United States Court of Appeals for the
Fifth Circuit. Order certifying interlocutory appeal entered May 31, 2023.
Johnson v. Guerrero , No. 23 -70002, United States Court of Appeals for the
Fifth Circuit. Panel opinion on certified question entered July 23, 2025. Order
denying rehearing en banc entered January 12, 2026.
There are no other proceedings directly related to this case.

1
OPINIONS AND O RDERS BELOW
The United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit’s  opinion answering
the certified question, namely “[w]hether there can be judicially created exceptions to
28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(2)(a),” is unpublished and unreported. The opinion is reproduced
at Pet. App. 1a–6a. The court’s order denying rehearing en banc is reported at 164
F.4th 398. That order is reproduced at Pet. App. 67a–73a.
The United States District Court for the Souther n District of Texas’s
memorandum and order addressing whether Mr. Johnson satisfied  28 U.S.C.
§ 2244(b)(2)(A)’s successive  petition requirements  is unpublished and unreported.
The memorandum and order are reproduced at Pet. App. 7a–46a.
The United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit’s opinion authorizing
Mr. Johnson to file a second or successive habeas application is reported at 935 F.3d
284. The opinion is reproduced at Pet. App. 47a–66a.
STATEMENT OF JURISDICTION
The court of appeals issued its decision on July 23, 2025, and denied rehearing
en banc on January 12, 2026.  On February 19, 2026, the Director petitioned for a
writ of certiorari. A motion to extend the time to file a response to the petition was
granted, extending the time to file this response to April 24, 2026. This Court has
jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1254(1).

2
STATUTORY PROVISIONS INVOLVED
28 U.S.C. § 2244(b) provides:
(1) A claim presented in a second or successive habeas corpus application under
section 2254 that was presented in a prior application shall be dismissed.
(2) A claim presented in a second or successive habeas corpus application under
section 2254 that was not presented in a prior application shall be dismissed unless—
(A) the applicant shows that the claim relies on a new rule of constitutional
law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that
was previously unavailable; or
(B)
(i) the factual predicate for the claim could not have been discovered
previously through the exercise of due diligence; and
(ii) the facts underlying the claim, if proven and viewed in light of the
evidence as a whole, would be sufficient to establish by clear and
convincing evidence that, but for constitutional error, no reasonable
factfinder would have found the applicant gui lty of the underlying
offense.
(3)
(A) Before a second or successive application permitted by this section is filed
in the district court, the applicant shall move in the appropriate court of
appeals for an order authorizing the district court to consider the application.
(B) A motion in the court of appeals for an order authorizing the district court
to consider a second or successive application shall be determined by a threejudge panel of the court of appeals.
(C) The court of appeals may authorize the filing of a second or successive
application only if it determines that the application makes a prima facie
showing that the application satisfies the requirements of this subsection.
(D) The court of appeals shall grant or deny the authorization to file a second
or successive application not later than 30 days after the filing of the motion.
(E) The grant or denial of an authorization by a court of appeals to file a second
or successive application shall not be appealable and shall not be the subject
of a petition for rehearing or for a writ of certiorari.
(4) A district court shall dismiss any claim presented in a second or successive
application that the court of appeals has authorized to be filed unless the applicant
shows that the claim satisfies the requirements of this section.

3
INTRODUCTION
Petitioner asks the Court to review a Fifth Circuit decision authorizing a
successive habeas claim that had no possibility of merit  at the time of the first
petition. The court below followed the same approach as other circuits  when
considering whether a claim was “previously unavailable” under the Antiterrorism
and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 ( AEDPA): a pragmatic approach that takes
into account the specific circumstances of the first habeas petition. Applying this test,
the Fifth Circuit correctly held that a claim was “previously unavailable” when it had
no possibility of merit at the time of the first habeas petition.
Petitioner claims this case “may well present the only vehicle to resolve the
issue.” Pet. 3. That assertion underscores  that the question presented is not
recurring. See Sup. Ct. R. 10. And it shows that it is not worth this Court’s time and
resources to resolve. Indeed, in the nearly thirty years since AEDPA took effect only
two habeas petitioners utilizing this “no possibility of merit” rule have received
preliminary circuit court authorization to proceed on a successive petition. Zero have
obtained relief from their conviction or sentence.
This case is also a poor vehicle for two reasons. It is interlocutory: Petitioner
can seek review of  the same question if a court should grant habeas relief . Second,
the petition asks th e Court to answer a question different from the one certified to
the court of appeals for interlocutory review.

STATEMENT OF THE C ASE
Procedural History
Conviction & Trial Record : In June 2007, a jury convicted
Respondent, Dexter Johnson, of capital murder and sentenced him to death for the
killing of Maria Aparece when Mr. Johnson was 18 years old. Pet. App. 2a. At
trial, Mr. Johnson presented Dr. Dale Watson’s testimony that his intellectual
functioning was roughly equivalent to that of a ten-year-old. Pet. App. 3a. Dr. Watson
calculated Mr. Johnson’s IQ to be between 74 and 88. Pet. App. 14a n.2 (citing Tr .
Vol. 31 at 204).
Because Mr. Johnson’s sco re was higher than 70, based upon the thenexisting diagnostic criteria, Dr. Watson testified that Mr. Johnson did not have an
intellectual disability. Id. The trial testimony showed that a claim under Atkins v.
Virginia, 536 U.S. 304 (2002), had no possibility of merit at that time.
After sentencing, the trial court appointed counsel to represent Mr. Johnson
in his state habeas proceedings. His appointed counsel did not raise an Atkins
claim. Pet. App. 14a. The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals affirmed Mr.
Johnson’s conviction and sentence on direct appeal. Pet. App. 69a; Johnson v.
State, 2010 WL 359018 (Tex. Crim. App. Jan. 27, 2010). It also denied his
initial state habeas application. Pet. App. 69a; Ex parte Johnson, 2010 WL 2617804
(Tex. Crim. App. June 30, 2010). This Court denied certiorari. Johnson v. Texas, 561
U.S. 1031 (2010).
Initial federal habe as: In June 2011, Mr. Johnson file d his initial federal
habeas petition in the Southern District of Texas without raising an Atkins claim or
4

5
asserting that he was intellectually disabled. Pet. App. 14a–15a (Johnson v. Stephens,
4-11-cv-2466, Dkt. Entry No. 1).
While Mr. Johnson’s initial federal habeas petition was pending, t he DSM-51
was published, which “ significantly altered how clinicians viewed the relationship
between IQ scores and intellectual disability.” Pet. App. 15a. It “recogniz[ed] that an
individual with an IQ score over 70 may still qualify as intellectually disabled.” Pet.
App. 15a (quoting In re Milam, 838 F. App’x 796, 799 (5th Cir. 2020)).
The Court has confirmed that Atkins determinations must be “informed by the
medical community’s diagnostic framework .” Hall v. Florida, 572 U.S. 701, 721
(2014); see Pet. App. 15a. Texas, however, continued applying its judge-made Briseno2
factors until this Court struck them down in 2017. Moore v. Texas, 581 U.S. 1 (2017).
On remand, the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals adopted the DSM -5 as the
governing standard but still denied relief. Ex parte Moore, 548 S.W.3d 552, 560 (Tex.
Crim. App. 2018) . This Court had to intervene a second time  to rectify Texas’
continued “failure to adhere closely enough to the psychological profession’s
standards” captured in the DSM-5. Pet. App 16a; Moore v. Texas, 586 U.S. 133, 139–
142 (2019).
1 American Psychiatric Association, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders  (5th ed.
2013) [hereinafter DSM-5]. The APA designates the Manual as the “DSM -5,” but courts in this case
have used “DSM-V.” This Brief follows the APA’s usage, but both terms refer to the same publication.
2 Ex parte Briseno, 135 S.W.3d 1, 8–9 (Tex. Crim. App. 2004) (setting forth seven “evidentiary factors”
for factfinders in the criminal context to consider in evaluating intellectual disability).

The district court denied Mr. Johnson’s petition  on August 19, 2013, shortly
after the DSM-5 was published and well before Texas adapted its standards to comply
with it . Pet.  App. 15a, 27a;  Johnson v. Stephens ¸ 2014 WL 2882365 (S.D. Tex.
June 25, 2014); Moore, 548 S.W.3d at 555. The Fifth Circuit affirmed, and this Court
again denied certiorari. Pet.  App. 69a; Johnson v. Stephens , 617 F. App ’x 293 (5th
Cir. 2015), cert. denied, 577 U.S. 1121 (2016).
Atkins claim : Mr. Johnson was set to be executed on May 2, 2019. Pet. App.
17a. He wrote to the federal district court raising concerns about his attorney, Patrick
McCann, and requesting new counsel, the Federal Public Defender (FPD). Pet. App.
17a, 49a. On February 5, 2019, the district court appointed the FPD as co-counsel
alongside McCann. Pet. App. 49a. The FPD eventually moved to remove McCann. Id.
On April 22, 2019, McCann filed  a successive state habeas application
asserting an Atkins claim for the first time based on an evaluation performed by Dr.
Greg Hupp on April 4. Dr. Hupp administered the WAIS-IV, obtained a full-scale IQ
score of 70, and evaluated Mr. Johnson’s adaptive functioning. Pet. App. 17a–18a. Dr.
Hupp concluded that Mr. Johnson meets the DSM -5 criteria “as a person with an
intellectual disability.” Id.
On April 29, 2019, the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals dismissed his
application as an abuse of the writ without reaching the merits. Ex parte Johnson ,
No. WR-73,600-02, 2019 WL 1915204 (Tex. Crim. App. Apr. 29, 2019) (per curiam).
The following day, the federal district court stayed Mr. Johnson’s May 2 execution ,
6

7
as requested by the FPD based on concerns about McCann’s representation, which
the Director did not appeal. Pet. App. 50a. McCann withdrew two days later, and the
State obtained a new execution date: August 15, 2019. Id.
With the rescheduled execution fast approaching, the FPD f iled a successive
state habeas application asserting an Atkins claim with an expanded record. Pet.
App. 17a–18a. Included with Mr. Johnson’s application was a comprehensive forensic
neuropsychological report from Dr. Daniel Martell, a declaration from Dr. Watson,
and additional supporting evidence not included in McCann’s earlier filing. Id.  Dr.
Martell found that Mr. Johnson has a frontal lobe impairment, right hemisphere
brain dysfunction, and is “at or below the bottom two percent of the population” for
verbal learning and memory. Pet. App. 61a– 62a. Dr. Martell  concluded that Mr.
Johnson met DSM -5 criteria for an intellectual disability. Id. Mr. Johnson’s
successive state application was dismissed. App. 18a; Ex parte Johnson, No. WR -
73,600-03, 2019 WL 3812803 (Tex. Crim. App. Aug. 13, 2019).
Mr. Johnson also  moved in the Fifth Circuit for authorization to file a
successive federal habeas application asserting an Atkins claim. In re Johnson, 935
F.3d 284 (5th Cir. 2019) ; Pet. App. 47a– 66a. In addition to  Dr. Martell’s and Dr.
Hupp’s conclusions, Mr. Johnson’s initial expert at trial, Dr. Watson, stated that his
prior testing “would not automatically preclude” an intellectual- disability diagnosis
under the new DSM-5 criteria and that he would no longer testify that Mr. Johnson
was not intellectually disabled. Pet. App. 18a–19a.

8
A Fifth Circuit panel authorized Mr. Johnson’s filing and stayed his execution.
Pet. App. 66a. Relying on In re Cathey , 857 F.3d 221 (5th Cir. 2017), the panel
reasoned that § 2244(b)(2)(A) permitted Mr. Johnson to assert an Atkins claim
because it was “previously unavailable” and the DSM -5’s “significant change . . . in
the medical methodology for evaluating the relevant disabilities” gave  it some
possibility of merit for the first time. Pet. App. 59a (reasoning it “is correct to equate
legal availability with changes in the standards for psychiatric evaluation of the key
intellectual disability factual issues”).
In March 2022, the district court held an evidentiary hearing to determine
whether Mr. Johnson satisfied AEDPA’s successive -petition requirements and
whether his claim was timely. Pet. App. 7a, 19a. The court found that Mr. Johnson
“had met the statutory requirements which would allow his Atkins claim to proceed
to adjudication.” Pet. App. 7a.
Petitioner moved the district court to certify three questions for interlocutory
appeal under 28 U.S.C. §  1292(b). Pet. App. 8a–9a. Only one relates to the question
presented here. The district court certified only that question, written by Petitioner:
“Whether there can be judicially created exceptions to 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(2)(A)?” Pet.
App. 8a.
Decision Below
The Fifth Circuit accepted the interlocutory appeal , and the same panel that
authorized Mr. Johnson’s successive application issued its decision on July 23, 2025.

9
Pet. App. 1a. That opinion was  not designated for publication under Fifth Circuit
Rule 47.5. Pet. App. 1a. It carries no precedential weight within the Fifth Circuit.
On Petitioner’s certified question, the panel answered: no, courts may not
create equitable exceptions to jurisdictional requirements contained in
§ 2244(b)(2)(A). Pet. App. 5a–6a. The panel held that Cathey created no such
exception but supplied the correct interpretation of “previously unavailable.” Pet.
App. 5a –6a (explaining “ [a] claim is not automatically considered previously
available” because it was conceivable; it must have had “some possibility of merit to
be considered available” (quoting Cathey, 857 F.3d at 232)). The Fifth Circuit denied
rehearing en banc. Pet. App. 67a–68a.
The lower courts have not adjudicated the merits of Mr. Johnson’s Atkins
claim, and no final judgment has been entered. In this unusual interlocutory posture,
the question presented is only whether AEDPA bars Mr. Johnson from continuing to
litigate his claim in federal court.
ARGUMENT
This case does not warrant the Court’s review. Lower courts follow a similar,
pragmatic standard to determine whether a claim was “previously unavailable .” In
this case, the Fifth Circuit applied the standard to Mr. Johnson’s Atkins claim
correctly. Moreover, the “no possibility of merit” question arises rarely, and this case
is a poor vehicle for resolving it.

10
I. The opinion below does not implicate a division of authority worth
resolution by this Court.
Petitioner claims that the decision below implicates an “acknowledged and
entrenched circuit split.” Pet. 12. The “acknowledge[ment]” refers to a single Eleventh
Circuit panel decision stating that it disagrees with the result in Johnson and Cathey.
In re Bowles, 935 F.3d 1210, 1219 (11th Cir. 2019).  The Petitioner’s assertion
overstates the conflict between the courts of appeals on the question presented.
Lower courts are not conflicted on the appropriate legal standard for
authorizing successive habeas claims—they uniformly apply a feasibility standard to
determine whether a habeas claim was “previously unavailable.” The feasibility
standard “takes into account the particular circumstances of the previous habeas
proceeding” to determine whether a claim was “previously unavailable.” Cathey, 857
F.3d at 229 (quoting In re Wood , 648 F.  App’x 388, 391 (5th Cir. 2016) ). The lower
courts Petitioner claims disagree have all rejected a strict rule in favor of this
pragmatic approach. In re Everett , 797 F.3d 1282, 1288 (11th Cir. 2015) ( using a
feasibility standard to determine previous unavailability in second or successive
habeas petitions); Cathey, 857 F.3d at 229 (adopting the Eleventh Circuit’s feasibility
standard to determine unavailability); Muñoz v. United States, 28 F.4th 973, 975–76
(9th Cir. 2022)  (following a “pragmatic approach” that considers whether, “as a
practical matter,” a habeas petitioner could have raised a claim in an earlier petition).
To be sure, the Fifth and Eleventh Circuits disagree over which factual
scenarios amount to a feasible claim. In the Fifth Circuit’s view, a habeas petitioner

11
can make a “prima facie showing that it was not feasible to amend his initial petition
to include a [claim for habeas relief]” when, at the time of the initial petition, the
claim had no possibility of merit. Cathey, 857 F.3d at  223. The Eleventh Circuit, by
contrast, does not consider “whether the claim would have been a winning one at the
time of the first petition,” opting instead to consider the timing of the retroactive rule
in relation to the initial habeas petition. Bowles , 935 F.3d at 1219. But c ourts of
appeals uniformly follow the same test, and a difference in mere application does not
warrant this Court’s review.
Petitioner attempts to frame the circuit split as one that implicates  a “futility
exception” or “ judicially created exception” to AEDPA’s bar on successive habeas
petitions. Pet. 14, 18. But there is no conflict on that question  either. Indeed, the
decision below expressly states that it does not recognize any futility exception  to
successive habeas claims. Pet. App. 5a (“Despite the label given by the State and the
district court, this court did not create any exceptions to the requirements of Section
2244(b)(2)(A) in Cathey.”). And for good reason. As the court below noted, courts have
“no authority to create equitable exceptions to jurisdictional requirements.”  Pet. App.
5a (quoting Bowles v. Russell , 551 U.S. 205, 214 (2007) ). Rather, the lower court
explained that its interpretation of the term “previously unavailable” was only that:
statutory interpretation, which is permissible “even [of] jurisdictional statutes like
Section 2244(b)(2)(A).” Pet. App. 6a (citing Tyler v. Cain , 533 U.S. 656, 662– 63
(2001)).

12
Even if framed as a split on the interpretation of AEDPA’s “previously
unavailable” standard, Petitioner overstates the conflict on that question. Only the
Fifth and Eleventh Circuits have directly addressed whether the merits of a prior
habeas petition should impact the inquiry into whether a claim was “previously
unavailable.” Cathey, 857 F.3d at 227–34; Bowles, 935 F.3d at  1215–21. And even
though the Eleventh Circuit considered the question, it did so only in dicta. Bowles ,
935 F.3d at 1219 (explaining that the “fundamental problem” with Bowles’ argument
is that it relied on Hall , which has not been made retroactive to cases on collateral
review, unlike Atkins).
The other circuits have little to no discussion of the merits of the underlying
claim. The issue in the Ninth Circuit was not the merits, but instead “challenges pro
se prisoners face when preparing legal filings.” Muñoz , 28 F.4th at 978 . The Fourth
Circuit case Petitioner cites address es the “no possibility of merit” issue in one
conclusory sentence, likely because the earlier petition was denied on the merits and
therefore raised the issue claimed to be “unavailable.” Slusser v. Vereen, 36 F.4th 590,
596 (4th Cir. 2022) . The Eighth Circuit, too, m erely made a passing reference to
“evidence” when considering the “previously unavailable” standard . Davis v. Norris,
423 F.3d 868, 879 (8th Cir. 2005). These cursory references, without any substantive
analysis as to whether the merits of a claim sho uld be considered, are not enough to
contribute to the alleged circuit split. As a result, t his Court should allow this issue
to percolate in the lower courts prior to intervention. See Baker v. City of McKinney,

13
Texas, 145 S. Ct. 11, 13 (2024) (Sotomayor, J., joined by Gorsuch, J., respecting  the
denial of certiorari) (“Only a few Courts of Appeals have weighed in [on the question
presented] . . . . [The question presented] is an important and complex question that
would benefit from further percolation in the lower courts prior to this Court’s
intervention.”).
These cases, and other authorities Petitioner relies on , relate to timing —not
the merits of a claim. Pet. 20. Those cases merely assumed, absent any rebuttal, that
a new constitutional rule was available so long as it had been published by the time
of the district court’s ruling on the first habeas petition. The Fifth Circuit agrees with
that approach. See Cathey, 857 F.3d at 229 ( “[Our previous  decision] essentially
adopted a rebuttable presumption that a new rule of constitutional law was
previously available if published by the time a district court ruled on a petitioner's
initial habeas petition.”). The authorities Petitioner cites regarding timing provide no
support for the alleged circuit split.
Finally, Petitioner claims that the alleged circuit split is “entrenched” because
neither the Fifth nor the Eleventh Circuit will reconsider its rule. Pet. 21. True,
AEDPA bars petitioning for rehearing en  banc of authorization decisions for state
prisoners. 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(3)(E). But it does not bar rehearing sua sponte. See In
re Byrd, 269 F.3d 585, 588 (6th Cir. 2001) ( Jones, J., concurring) (explaining that
§ 2244(b)(3)(E) does not “alter the authority of the en banc court to order a rehearing
on its own motion”). It also does not bar petitioning for rehearing by federal prisoners,

14
a circumstance which occurred in several of the cases creating the alleged circuit split.
Bowe v. United States, 146 S. Ct. 447, 462 (2026)  (“[F]ederal prisoners are not
prohibited from seeking certiorari from a panel ’s denial of authorization to file a
second or successive motion.”) ; Muñoz, 28 F.4th at 974 (addressing a successive
§ 2255 motion); Slusser, 36 F.4th at 592 ( resolving a § 2241 motion by a federal
prisoner, who previously filed a successive § 2255 petition) . And even if rehearing of
the authorization decision is as limited as Petitioner claims, those limitations do not
apply to the merits determination that inevitably follows authorization. There are
plenty of routes for lower courts to consider this issue for the first time or reconsider
their rule on the matter.
Accordingly, there is no conflict among lower courts warranting the Court’s
review.
II. This case is fact-bound and the peculiar circumstances in this case
arise infrequently.
The question presented arises  infrequently and is not important enough to
warrant this Court’s attention. Petitioner admits exactly that when he argues that
this case presents a rare opportunity for this Court to resolve it. Pet. 29. That only
two petitioners—Mr. Johnson and the prisoner in Cathey—in the nearly thirty years
since the passage of AEDPA have received circuit authorization on this issue shows
how rare it is. And neither has actually received relief yet, as both of their cases are
still pending. Given  the narrowness of the Fifth Circuit’s interpretation of

§ 2244(b)(2)(A) and AEDPA’s multitude of hur dles f or habea s r elief, the question
presented is seldom decisive.
First, consider the narrowness of the rule. The prisoner’s claim must rest on a
new rule of constitutional law made retroactive by the Supreme Court which was
previously unavailable because it lacked any “possibility of merit.” Cathey, 857 F .3d
at 230, 232. The universe of cases this rule could possibly apply to is already smal l
because there are few  new rules of constitutional law  in habeas cases . And on ly a
small subset of these new rules —substantive, no t procedural rules—a re made
retroactive. Edwards v.  Vannoy, 593 U.S. 255, 264 & n.3 (2021).  Those substantive
rules are ones which “forbid[] criminal punishment o f certain primary conduct” or
“prohibit[] a certain category of punishment for a class of defendants because of their
status or offense.” Montgomery v. Louisiana, 577 U.S. 190, 198 (2016) (quoting Penry
v. Lynaugh, 492 U.S. 302, 330 (1989), overruled by  Atkins, 536 U.S. 304).  The rule
from Atkins is one of the few.
Next, even with a new, retroactive decision, the Fifth Circuit’s rule opens the
door to pursue relief only  in rare situations . A habeas petitioner’s claim, which
previously lacked  any “possibility of merit ,” must have become  a “possible claim”
because the framework for analyzing it changed around the time o r after their first
application was denied. Pet. App. 58a–59a (quoting Cathey, 857 F.3d at 232). In the
context of an Atkins  claim, t he switch  which  turn s the claim from meritless to
meritorious is not mere new factfinding or “a reassessment by medical professionals
15

16
of [an] inmate’s particular mental abilities .” Pet. App. 59a. Instead,  “the significant
change [is] in the medical methodology for evaluating the relevant disabilities and in
courts’ recognition of those changes.” Id.
Mr. Johnson’s is the rare case. The DSM-5 contained “significant changes in
the diagnosis of intellectual disability” and was published just 17 days before his first
habeas application was denied . Id. Before the DSM -5’s publication and acceptance ,
Mr. Johnson’s Atkins claim had “no possibility of merit.” But because the criteria for
assessing intellectual disability has changed, his claim now has possible merit.
Unsurprisingly, other petitioners have failed to fit Atkins  claims in their
successive habeas applications within the “no possibility of merit” rule . See In re
Soliz, 938 F.3d 200, 203– 04 (5th Cir. 2019) (denying leave to file successive
application on Atkins  claim because petitioner failed to show that there was a
meaningful change in the medical  field’s analysis of fetal alcohol spectrum disorder
as equated to intellectual disability under Atkins); In re Milam, 838 F. App’x 796, 799
(5th Cir. 2020) (denying leave to file successive application when an Atkins claim was
feasible during first application under the pre-DSM-5 regime).
Second, AEDPA imposes numerous additional barriers to successive
applications that sink prisoners’ claims seeking to benefit from the narrow “no
possibility of merit” rule.  Applications raising claims that were raised in a prior
application must be dismissed. 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(1). Additionally, AEDPA imposes
a limitations period on successive claims. § 2244(d).

17
All these hurdles exist before a court even reaches the merits of the habeas
claim. Mr. Johnson’s claim has  not yet been resolved. It is too early to tell whether
the Fifth Circuit’s interpretation of § 2244(b)(2)(A) has ever made a difference in the
ultimate disposition of  a single habeas claim. The question does not warrant this
Court’s review at this time.
III. This case is also a poor vehicle because  it comes in an  interlocutory
posture and seeks review of  a different question than the district
court certified.
The Petition comes in an unusual posture that makes it a poor candidate for
certiorari. The district court certified  an interlocutory appeal under § 1292(b). Had
this case proceeded to merits review of  the Atkins claim after the district court’s
decision in 2022, an evidentiary hearing on the merits of the Atkins claim would have
been completed by now, allowing the normal course of the merits and procedural
questions being considered together on appeal.  This Court is hesitant to take cases
from an interlocutory order rather than final judgment. See Sup. Ct. R. 11; Harrel v.
Raoul, 144 S. Ct. 2491, 2492 (2024) (statement of Thomas, J.) (“This Court is rightly
wary of taking cases in an interlocutory posture.”); Abbott v. Veasey, 580 U.S. 1104,
1105 (2017) (Roberts, C.J., respecting the denial of certiorari ) (noting that a case is
“better suited for certiorari review” after final judgment and not in an interlocutory
posture); Mount Soledad Mem ’l Ass’n v. Trunk, 567 U.S. 944, 945 (2012) (Alito, J.,
respecting the denial of certiorari) (agreeing with denial of certiorari when a petition
came in an “interlocutory posture”).  At this stage in the litigation, it is uncertain

18
whether the question presented will control the final outcome of Mr. Johnson’s
petition. Mr. Johnson’s habeas petition should continue to final judgment.
Texas has opposed certiorari in scenarios  before final judgment in federal
habeas proceedings. In cases  where a prisoner petitions for certiorari to review the
denial of his state habeas claims while a federal habeas claim is pending, Texas has
urged this Court to deny certiorari before the federal proceedings have completed. See
Brief in Opposition  at 13, Uvukansi v. Texas, 142 S. Ct. 2811 (2022 ) (No. 21-151),
2021 WL 5513772, at *13. It has even made the same argument when the federal
avenue is unlikely to allow the Court to  reach the question, like where AEDPA’s
statute of limitations bars the claim.  See Brief in Opposition at 11– 12, Santana v.
Texas, 144 S. Ct. 546 (2024) (No. 22- 1139), 2023 WL 8112707, at *11– 12. Now
Petitioner makes the inverse argument: grant certiorari before federal proceedings
have rendered a final judgment because it may be hard to reach the question
otherwise.
And contra Petitioner’s suggestion, taking this case on interlocutory review is
not the only way for the Court to answer this question.  The Court can wait for final
judgment in this case. Or it can review a certification decision by a court of appeals
on a successive application from a prisoner in federal custody. Federal prisoner claims
based on previously unavailable constitutional rules  are governed by substantially
similar language as state prisoners, § 2255(h)(2), and are not subject to the certiorari
bar that state custody claims are, § 2244(b)(3)(E).

19
Another wrinkle in this case that shows that it is a poor vehicle to review the
question presented is that  Petitioner asks this Court to decide a different question
than the one he asked the district court to certify  for interlocutory review. Upon
Petitioner’s request, the district court certified the question “[w]hether there can be
judicially created exceptions to 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(2)(A).” See Pet. App. 8a. The Fifth
Circuit answered in the negative.  Pet. App. 5a . Petitioner does not dispute that
answer but instead disagrees with the Fifth Circuit’s decision not to overrule Cathey
and Johnson.  While a § 1292(b) appeal gives this Court jurisdiction over the order
and not only the certified question, the Court should not reward Petitioner for failing
to present his real issue in the certified order. Cf. Clark v. Sweeney, 607 U.S. 7 (2025).
IV. The lower court was correct.
AEDPA provides that a prisoner may bring a second or successive habeas claim
if the applicant can show that the claim “relies on a new rule of constitutional law
made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court,  that was
previously unavailable.” 28 U.S.C. §  2244(b)(2)(A). As the district court observed,
“Atkins unquestionably created a new rule of constitutional law . . . [and] Atkins was
made retroactive on federal habeas review.” Pet. App. 23a. And in the decision below,
the Fifth Circuit relied on its definition of “previously unavailable” as applied in
Cathey. This interpretation was correct.
The Court has interpreted “available” in the context of the Prison Litigation
Reform Act (PLRA) . Booth v. Churner , 532 U.S. 731, 737– 38 (2001); Ross v. Blake ,
578 U.S. 632, 642 (2016)). In those cases, the Court adopted the ordinary meaning of

20
“available,” which means “‘capable of use for the accomplishment of a purpose, ’ and
that which ‘ is accessible or may be obtained .’” Booth, 532 U.S. at 737–38 (quoting
Webster’s Third New International Dictionary 150 (1993) ); Ross, 578 U.S. at 642. A
similar approach is called for here regarding the interpretation of “unavailable” in
AEDPA. See A. Scalia & B. Garner, Reading Law  § 25, at 170–73 (2012) (discussing
how the presumption of consistent usage can apply to statutes that are “enacted at
the same time, and deal[] with the same subject”).
Unavailability must be interpreted functionally . When a claim has “no
possibility of merit,” it cannot “be obtained.” See Booth, 532 U.S. at 737–38 (quoting
Webster’s Third New International Dictionary 150 (1993)) . Determining whether a
claim is “available” requires a consideration of “real-world workings.” Ross, 578 U.S.
at 643. Solutions which “operate[] as a simple dead end” or are, “practically speaking,
incapable of use,” are unavailable. Id.
Mr. Johnson’s Atkins claim was not available when he filed his first application
for habeas relief in federal court.  Despite Atkins being a new rule of constitutional
law made retroactive by this Court, it required the publication of the DSM-5 to have
any possibility of merit. And Texas courts  (which establish the substantive Atkins
standard which federal courts must follow for Texas cases)  did not adopt the DSM-5
as the governing criteria for an Atkins claim until 2018—nearly seven years after Mr.
Johnson’s initial federal habeas petition. Moore , 548 S.W.3 d at 555. Because Mr.

21
Johnson’s Atkins claim was functionally unavailable, the Fifth Circuit  correctly
authorized his successive petition.
CONCLUSION
The Court should deny the petition for a writ of certiorari.
